title: The blind man's jewel
hookLine: a thrift-store find you weren't looking for; Shantideva calls the awakening mind a jewel found in a rubbish heap
tomorrow: jewel in hand. what does he promise next?
last: A BRIDGE, A BOAT, A LAMP.

lines: THE BOTTOM OF A THRIFT BIN.
cards: Somebody digs through the bottom of a thrift-store bin, mostly to kill time, and pulls out a jacket that fits like it was made for them. Four dollars. They weren't looking for it.
They couldn't have planned it. If they'd come an hour later, someone else would be wearing it. That's yesterday's question, almost.
How does a blind man find a jewel in the trash? The same way: not by looking. So, one question for today: what do you do with something good you didn't earn?

teach.h: A BLIND MAN, A JEWEL, A RUBBISH HEAP.
teach.b: Near the end of chapter three, Shantideva says: like a blind man finding a jewel in a heap of rubbish, so, by some chance, this awakening mind has arisen in me. He doesn't take credit.

teach.h: BY SOME CHANCE, IT AROSE IN ME.
teach.b: The wish to wake up for everyone, the thing this whole poem is about, showed up in him the way a jewel turns up under a blind man's hand.
Then he can't stop naming it: a nectar that ends death, a treasure that never runs out, a tree to rest under, the moon, the sun. Christian neighbors know this feeling from a parable of Jesus.
In the King James English: "the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field." A man finds it and, the verse says, for joy goes and sells all he has to buy that field.

Shared ground: the best thing is found more than made, and the right answer to finding it is joy, then giving everything to keep it. One honest difference: in the parable the treasure is the kingdom of heaven.
For Shantideva the jewel is a state of his own mind, the wish to awaken for all beings, arising in him. Two treasures, two fields, and the same astonished joy.

how: Tibetan teachers sometimes quote this verse when students first take up the awakening mind, as a reminder to treat the wish as precious and not as an achievement.

games.q: what does “the blind man's jewel” mean?
o: a gem that blind monks wear as a sign of rank
a priceless good found by chance, not by skill
a reward given to the one who works the hardest

games.q: two found treasures — tap the pairs.
p: finds a jewel in a rubbish heap
the awakening mind, arisen by chance
for joy sells all he has

s: Shantideva says he earned the awakening mind by his own skill
he says it arose in him by some chance, like a jewel under a blind man's hand.
Jesus tells a parable of treasure hidden in a field
a man finds it and, for joy, sells all he has to buy the field (Matthew 13:44).
the parable and the verse are about the same treasure
both meet a found treasure with joy, but the parable's is the kingdom of heaven; Shantideva's is the awakening mind.

games.q: a teacher you never asked for turned your year around. what fits Shantideva's verse?
o: take credit; you did the work, so it was really all you.
treasure it as a found jewel: be glad, and let it shape what you do.
shrug it off; luck isn't worth thinking about.
games.why: Shantideva doesn't claim the jewel or ignore it. found by chance, it's treasured, and in the next verses it shapes his whole life.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one lucky thing in your life you didn't earn: a person, a place, a chance, a teacher, a day. Hold it the way you'd hold something just found in a heap.
Let yourself be glad, and stay with that gladness until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The blind man's jewel: Shantideva's picture of the awakening mind arising in him, found by chance, not by skill, and treasured.

orig.note: Sanskrit: jewel, gem. Buddhists also call the Buddha, dharma and sangha the Three Jewels (triratna).

carryVoice: The line: a jewel in the heap, found, not earned, and worth keeping. Fourteen days into the poem.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 3.27-3.32 (like a blind man finding a jewel in a heap of rubbish; the awakening mind as nectar, treasure, tree, moon, sun)
